mechaber.1#main: Laws of bishul akum. It contains 16 seifim: A food that is not eaten in its raw state, and also is fit to be served on a king's table to dip bread in it or as relish — if a non-Jew cooked it, even in a Jewish vessel and in a Jewish home, it is forbidden because of bishul akum.
mechaber.2#main: If one mixed a food eaten in its raw state with a food not eaten in its raw state and a non-Jew cooked them — if the main component is from something that has [the prohibition of] bishul akum, it is forbidden; if not, it is permitted. {Rama: And it is permitted to eat roasted peas of a non-Jew, and likewise legumes called arabshin roasted, for they are not served on a king's table; and so they practiced leniency with them, except in a place where they practice greasing the pan with milk — then they practice prohibition with them (Rambam chapter 17 of Hilchot Maachalot Assurot, Mahara of Prague, and glosses of the Arukh). But without this it is permitted, and one need not be concerned for the intestines of non-Jews, for usually they are not same-day [slaughter]. And any fruit eaten raw — even if a non-Jew cooked it and it dissolved and became a dish in their hands — is permitted; and therefore they eat compote that non-Jews make (private opinion from the implication of Rambam, Ran, and Tosafot, and it is straightforward).}
mechaber.3#main: Pastida that a non-Jew baked is forbidden, even for one who practices leniency with bread of a non-Jew, because the fat is forbidden while still visible because of bishul akum and is absorbed in the bread; and likewise vegetables eaten raw that were cooked with meat are forbidden because the fat of the meat is absorbed in them.
mechaber.4#main: There are those who permit with our maidservants, and there are those who forbid, even b'dieved (responsum of the Rashba, siman 68). {Rama: And b'dieved one may rely on the words of those who permit (Arukh, general rule 43, and glosses of ShaDa). And even l'chatchila they practice leniency in a Jewish home where maidservants and slaves cook in a Jewish home, because it is impossible that one of the household will not stoke [the fire] a little (there).}
mechaber.5#main: A non-Jew who cooked and did not intend for cooking is permitted. How so? A non-Jew who kindled a fire in a marsh to pass through the reeds and locusts were cooked in it — behold, these are permitted, even in a place where they are served on a king's table. And likewise if he singed the head to pass the hair — it is permitted to eat the tips of the ears that were roasted at the time of the singeing. But if he intended for cooking — for example, he kindled the oven to cook in it and there was meat in it at first and it was roasted — even though he did not intend for this meat, since he did not know of it, it is forbidden.
mechaber.6#main: Anything that a Jew cooked a little of its cooking, whether at the beginning or at the end, is permitted. Therefore, if a non-Jew placed meat or a pot on the fire and a Jew turned over the meat and stirred the pot, or a Jew stirred and a non-Jew finished — behold, this is permitted. (And even if it would not have cooked without the aid of the non-Jew.)
mechaber.7#main: Heating the oven (meaning: heating, heating up, and kindling — Onkelos: veyahon shagrin) is not effective except for bread; but for other cooked foods, heating the oven and lighting the fire do not raise or lower [the prohibition] — only placing [the food] specifically. Therefore, one who wishes to cook in a pan in a non-Jew's oven must have a Jew place the pan into the oven in the place fit for it to cook. {Rama: And there are disputants who hold that lighting the fire or stoking coals is effective for cooking as for bread, and so is the practice (glosses of ShaDa, Arukh general rule 43, and Mordechai, chapter of Avodah Zarah). And even stoking without intention is effective and helps (from the implication of Maharai in glosses of ShaDa and Kol Bo). And some say that even if a Jew did not stoke and did not throw a chip there, but only the non-Jew lit the fire from a Jew's fire — it is permitted (Issur ve-Heter there in the name of Maharam).}
mechaber.8#main: A Jew placed a pot on the fire and removed it, and a non-Jew came and returned it — it is forbidden, unless it had reached maachal ben drusai, which is one-third of its cooking when he removed it.
mechaber.9#main: If a non-Jew cooked it as maachal ben drusai and a Jew finished it — there is [reason] to forbid, unless it is erev Shabbos or erev Yom Tov, or there is great loss in the matter. (And there are those who permit in every case) (Tur in the name of the Rosh, Ran, Rif, Maharam, Issur ve-Heter, and Semak siman 223 — R' Yakar did so in practice; and so in Kol Bo; and so in Semak, Mordechai, Agudah, chapter of Avodah Zarah, and Rae in Sefer Beit Hashem; and Semag daf 57 side 2; and so received from Maran and R' Yerucham, section 17 chapter 7 — for so agreed most poskim, and not as the Beit Yosef challenged in Beit Hashem on R' Yerucham in this — see there). And so is the practice.
mechaber.10#main: A Jew placed [food] on glowing coals where it was not fit to cook on them as maachal ben drusai, and a non-Jew came and turned it over and it cooked — it is forbidden.
mechaber.11#main: A Jew placed [food] on the fire and left a non-Jew to guard it, and he turned it over, and it is not known whether the non-Jew removed it before it reached maachal ben drusai — it is permitted. (For a doubt in their [rabbinic] matters is resolved leniently.) (Tur.) And likewise every doubt in bishul akum and the like is permitted.
mechaber.12#main: Small fish that a Jew or a non-Jew salted — behold, they are as though partially cooked; and if a non-Jew afterward roasted them, they are permitted. But large salted fish are not eaten except by pressing; therefore, if a non-Jew roasted them, they are forbidden. And there are those who permit. {Rama: And likewise anything eaten raw by pressing — if a non-Jew cooked it, its law is like large fish (private opinion). And salted meat is not eaten at all as it is raw, and it is forbidden if cooked by a non-Jew (Tosafot, chapter of Chalitzah).}
mechaber.13#main: A fish that a non-Jew salted, and fruits that they treated until they made them fit to eat — behold, these are permitted, for salting is not like boiling in this decree, and smoking is not like cooking. {Rama: Pickling too is not like cooking, for they only forbade cooking by fire (Tur).}
mechaber.14#main: An egg — even though it is fit to be swallowed raw — if a non-Jew cooked it, it is forbidden.
mechaber.15#main: Dates that are somewhat bitter, which are not eaten except by pressing — if a non-Jew cooked them, they are forbidden.
mechaber.16#main: Vessels in which a non-Jew cooked before us things that have [the prohibition of] bishul akum require kashering. And some say they do not require it. And even according to those who require kashering — if it is an earthenware vessel, one purges it three times and that suffices, because this prohibition has no Torah root. {Rama: A non-Jew who cooked for a sick person on Shabbos — it is permitted after Shabbos even for a healthy person, and there is no [prohibition] of bishul akum in it, for in every such case there is publicity (Beit Yosef in the name of the Ran, who so wrote in the name of the Rae).}

mateh-yehonatan.1#_: (Siman 113 in the Shulchan Aruch, seif 6 in the gloss.) And even if it would not cook, etc. See Taz, small note 6, and Shach, small note 8, in what they challenge — that this ruling is against the Gemara. And understand: that which the Gemara says that if it would not cook without the aid of gentiles it is forbidden — where a Jew does not do a complete action, but only the Jew places it on the fire and a non-Jew comes and turns it over — if so, the Jew does nothing and it is as if the non-Jew placed it on the fire from the outset without any aid of a Jew; not so when a Jew does a complete action, such as stirring it in such a case — the aid of a non-Jew forbids nothing. Investigate.
mateh-yehonatan.2#_: (There, seif 8.) A Jew placed a pot on the fire, etc. See Shach, small note 12. And behold, the proof of the Bach is that one must say that if a non-Jew removed it, then there is no [prohibition] of bishul akum in it; for otherwise it would be difficult — that which we say in the chapter of Avodah Zarah, daf 38 side 1, there: for example, he placed it on a tile and the non-Jew took it and placed it in the oven, etc. And it is impossible according to the Rashba's view; if so, it should have stated a greater novelty that even if the non-Jew himself removed it and returned and placed it in the oven — or that it is not forbidden thereby. And one must say that the Rashba holds that the Gemara did not descend to teach us only the law itself, that where the end of the cooking comes through a non-Jew it is forbidden, and it only used the language of placing on a tile; but in truth it is a dispute, and even if the non-Jew alone removed it, it is likewise forbidden. And the proof of the Rashba is from what it says in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah, daf 12: I did not go to draw water from your spring, and I saw a Jew and a non-Jew who cooked two pots, etc., and the Sages were not concerned because of bishul akum. And the Rashba explained that there is room to be concerned lest the non-Jew removed the pot and returned it on the fire; and from now one must say that even if the non-Jew alone removed and returned it, it is likewise forbidden. And the Bach must say that he explains like Rashi, that all the concern is lest he come to cook l'chatchila without aid. [Gloss: And from the words of the Rashba in Torat HaBayit, house 3, gate 7, it appears that he does not explain thus; for if so, he should have brought from there that we are not concerned lest a non-Jew removed it, and he need not have brought from that in chapter 2 of a Jew who placed, etc. Investigate. End of gloss of the great rabbi, our teacher R' Shlomo HaKohen, may his light shine, of Vilna.]
mateh-yehonatan.3#_: (There, seif 16.) Vessels in which a non-Jew cooked, etc. And some are stringent that it is not necessary, etc. They challenge this from above, siman 112 seif 6, where the Mechaber wrote regarding ipinadeh that a non-Jew baked — that it is forbidden even though there is only absorbed [taste]; and if so, it is proven that absorbed [taste] is forbidden in a kli rishon, and he brought no distinction in this. And it appears one could say that it is not comparable to above, for there there is absorption of the dish in the bread itself, and such a case is what there is room to be concerned for; not so where there is only absorption in the pot — if so, the dish cooked afterward in this pot has only absorption of absorption, and for so much they did not decree because of bishul akum. However, the Tur in this siman includes the law of absorption in the dish itself and absorption in the pot in one stroke, and it appears he has no such distinction. And one must say that certainly there is room to dispute such a case; and that which we included them is in min b'mino; but in a different species where the taste is recognizable, certainly in such a case he forbids because of bishul akum — investigate. But the implication of the Tur's words does not appear thus, for behold he wrote explicitly: the same applies to vegetables cooked with meat — investigate.

nekudot-hakesef.1#_: (Siman 113, in Taz, small note 2.) Already the Derishah and the Bach preceded him in all this — see there.
nekudot-hakesef.2#_: (There, in Taz, small note 15.) And there is further proof from siman 112, etc. This is not proof, for it is different here, for in every such case there is publicity and the decree of [intermarriage] feasts does not apply — know that that which is above in siman 112 itself is from the words of the Rae in Bedek HaBayit. And what he wrote: and if the Beit Yosef and Rama had seen, etc. — it is not so, for even if they had seen they could have ruled thus, for in a dispute of scribes we follow the lenient view, especially with bread of a non-Jew which is very lenient; and moreover the Ran's view in his responsum is like the Rae; and what is written in Beit Yosef at the end of siman 123 is mistaken, as written below at the end of siman 123 — see there.

pitchei-teshuva.1#_: That it is raw. The Avodat HaTaharah of Maharait wrote that the essence of the decree was because of [intermarriage] feasts, etc.; and see in Sefer Tiferet Moshe, who wrote that according to this reason the cooking of an apostate is permitted, for there is no [concern of] feasts (see above, siman 112, what is written there); except that there was another reason explained in Beit Yosef, lest he feed him forbidden things; and accordingly, the cooking of an apostate is also forbidden, for he is like a denier of the entire Torah and lest he feed him forbidden things — see there. And accordingly, the same applies to an apostate who desecrates Shabbos in public, or [denies] the entire Torah except for two [commandments], whose law is like a non-Jew, as above siman 2 seif 5, and below siman 119 — his cooking is likewise forbidden.
pitchei-teshuva.2#_: Stoking coals is effective. See in the responsa of the Radbaz, the new ones, siman 3.
pitchei-teshuva.3#_: In every case. Avodat HaTaharah; and see in Sefer Tiferet Moshe, who wrote that nevertheless, if a non-Jew cooked it as maachal ben drusai and removed it from the fire and returned — whether that non-Jew or another non-Jew — and finished it, it is forbidden. And some say regarding small fish that a non-Jew salted and returned and roasted them — below seif 12, that for salting they did not decree; but here the beginning and end are in the hand of a non-Jew — what difference is there whether in one action or that he took it in the interim? However, if a Jew took it from the fire and a non-Jew returned it — requires study; so too his conclusion — see there.
pitchei-teshuva.4#_: And so is the practice. And in Shlah, daf 76, he wrote that one should be stringent like Maharshal, that it does not help after cooking from maachal ben drusai — see there.
pitchei-teshuva.5#_: By pressing. Avodat HaTaharah; and see in the responsum Mayim Rabim from siman 15 through siman 20, see there, to permit chestnuts and lupines — see there well.
pitchei-teshuva.6#_: For a healthy person. Avodat HaTaharah; and see in Eshel Avraham what he wrote regarding the vessels. And in Sefer Chochmat Adam, klal 66, halachah 12, he wrote that one should permit the vessels after twenty-four hours even without hagalah — see there; and see in Chayei Adam, klal 69, halachah 16.

rabbi-akiva-eiger-yd.1#_: (Siman 113, seif 3.) And it is absorbed in the bread. And even though it is nullified in the majority, as above (siman 112, seif 4) in the gloss — here it is worse, for the fat is visible and recognizable in the bread, and it is like that case above (siman 112, seif 6) in the gloss of Minchat Yaakov (Kaf HaChayim, small note 226).
rabbi-akiva-eiger-yd.2#_: (Seif 9, in the gloss.) And they permit in every case. And one requires actual finishing; but not mere turning over. Derishah.

yad-avraham.1#_: (Siman 113, seif 16.) Vessels in which a non-Jew cooked, etc. Even according to those who require kashering — if it is an earthenware vessel, one purges it three times and that suffices, because this prohibition has no Torah root. In Be'er HaGolah he showed his source from the words of the Rashba — investigate: in Niddah, chapter of HaSefinah, he wrote in the name of the Rashba that even in a matter that has no Torah root they did not permit except for terumah, which is a rabbinic prohibition that is not equal in all respects. And so there in the name of the Rambam, who wrote that one does not learn from terumah to other rabbinic prohibitions. And see in Ketzot HaChoshen in explanation of Yerushalmi Pesachim, who challenged that in Yerushalmi there Rav said thus regarding chametz on Pesach for cooking — hagalah in boiling water is effective three times, even though it has a Torah root.

yad-ephraim.1#_: And if they roasted them. Avodat HaTaharah; and in responsa Be'er Mayim Chayim, Yoreh De'ah siman 254.
yad-ephraim.2#_: By pressing. Avodat HaTaharah; and responsa Avkat Rokhel siman 134: wheat that gentiles parboil until it reaches maachal ben drusai and return and dry them to make groats — and again they are not eaten except through further cooking — they are permitted, since they are dried so much that they are not eaten except through further cooking and the first cooking is not recognizable in them — see there. And see responsa Mayim Rabim, volume 4, from siman 15 through siman 19, on permitting chestnuts and lupines that gentiles cooked in their intestines, that there is no [prohibition] of bishul akum or gentile vessels; and there a responsum from one who challenged this, and the author returned and answered him — see there.
yad-ephraim.3#_: And smoked. Avodat HaTaharah; and in responsa Shevut Yaakov, volume 3, siman 74: a non-Jew who gave a Jew a gift of smoked fish — there is no concern of prohibition because they were smoked on his stove on which he cooks his foods, as we are not concerned for the smoking of a Jew to say concern that meat was smoked over milk cooking, as written in Terumat HaDeshen siman 13, since the hand is not scalded by steam — even though there is room to distinguish, etc. And that which they buy small fish called piketig that are smoked — one could say an oven has a special place for smoke; not so a non-Jew homeowner who smokes on his stove. Nevertheless, there is some proof from what they permit smoked [fish] because of bishul akum and they did not mention concern of steam, for we do not maintain a prohibition; also gentiles are careful not to smoke near a dish lest steam rise from the dish. And nevertheless, to distance from the smell of prohibition — lest he hung it to smoke with other meat or non-kosher fish and touched the prohibition itself — one should rinse the smoked meat again three times in alternating waters; and such a case is explained in Orach Chayim siman 447 regarding dried meat — see there.

turei-zahav.1#_: A food that is not eaten, etc. The reason is that the essence of the decree is because of [intermarriage] feasts, and a thing that is not so important — a person does not invite his friend for it.
turei-zahav.3#_: Pastida that a non-Jew baked, etc. In the Tur it is written: pastida of a non-Jew. And Beit Yosef wrote that it is a scribal error — why specify of a non-Jew? Even of a Jew too, for bishul akum [applies] even in a Jew's [dish] — end of his words. And it is astounding according to his words: why did the Tur and Shulchan Aruch conclude "even for one who practices leniency with bread of a non-Jew"? And with bread of a Jew, there is no one who permits if a non-Jew baked without a Jew's stoking, as the Tur wrote in siman 112. And if we deal with stoking, the fat too should not be forbidden, for bread of a Jew has the law of parched grain; and so I saw in the gloss of Semak siman 207. And these are its words: and if they did not make it fit with a chip, even the pastida itself is forbidden without absorption of fat, for although they permitted bread of a non-Jew, nevertheless bread of a Jew that a non-Jew baked without kashering the oven is forbidden — until here his language; therefore the text "pastida of a non-Jew" is more correct. But in Asheri and Mordechai, chapter of These Terefot, it is written explicitly: pastida of a Jew of fish that a non-Jew baked, etc. And it is astounding as we remembered; and some wish to resolve that we deal where they made the oven fit with a chip or stoking, and this helps for bread but not for a dish, as Beit Yosef wrote in this siman in the name of the Ran — and this is not so, for Mordechai explicitly explained in the chapter of Ein Ma'amidin, and the Rama brought below that throwing into a dish — stoking helps as for bread. And one must press and say that "of a Jew" that he cited refers to fish where they bought the fish from a Jew so there is no prohibition because of forbidden fish, but the dough itself is of a non-Jew and there was no kashering of the oven — therefore it is forbidden because of the fat of the fish. Afterward I found in Asheri of my elder R' Yitzchak bar Bezalel, may his memory be blessed, who erased those two words "of a Jew," and so it appears to me as primary that we deal with cooking of a non-Jew. And what Beit Yosef challenged — "even of a Jew" — he was not precise in this challenge, for the main novelty is since it was cooked by a non-Jew and the place is where they practice leniency with bread of gentiles — automatically one might think there is no prohibition in the fat too, for flour is primary, as I wrote before; it teaches us that here we do not say so, since the fat is visible and is not nullified. And so he wrote afterward regarding vegetables that they are permitted because of bishul akum, and one might think the reason of meat absorbed in them is secondary and nullified in the vegetables — it teaches us that not so; and if so, our author could not have omitted "of a Jew," for then both would be forbidden without this novelty. So it appears to me clearly. And I saw written that in fat of goose or of animal there is no prohibition of bishul akum, for usually it is already rendered and there is no cooking after cooking.
turei-zahav.4#א: With our maidservants. He explains: those acquired by us, and we are warned about their labor on Shabbos from the Torah; they are not included among this. Not gentile maidservants hired to a Jew for a term; but in Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, he wrote to permit with these too b'dieved and to rely on R' Avraham whom the Tur brings, that in a Jewish home there is no [prohibition of] bishul akum, even though we do not rule like him.
turei-zahav.4#ב: For it is impossible that he will not stoke, etc. Darkei Moshe wrote that we learn from here that even if he did not intend to permit through this stoking but did it without intention, it is permitted; and so too in Kol Bo — end of his words; and so too the Rama here below; and in Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, he wrote: but one should be careful that this stoking should help repair the fire and help hasten its cooking by a Jew — end of his words.
turei-zahav.5#_: Even though he did not intend, etc. In the Tur it is written: therefore, if he knew there was meat in the oven, even if they heated it to dry a vessel in it, it is forbidden — we are concerned lest he also intended for cooking. It is difficult for me: behold, the Tur wrote afterward in this siman that if a non-Jew turned it over and it is not known whether he removed it, etc., we are not concerned lest he removed it, for a doubt in their matters is lenient; if so, a fortiori here, for there we see the non-Jew did the act of turning over, and even so we are not concerned for prohibition — a fortiori here. And one could answer that there the non-Jew has no benefit, as Beit Yosef wrote in the name of the Rashba — if so, even by Torah law we would be lenient, as below siman 118 seif 10; and this is truly the Rashba's intent when he wrote "and moreover," etc. But on the Tur it is difficult, and one must press and distinguish that the case of removal is different, for it is not so common to do as here, where it is common to also intend for cooking.
turei-zahav.6#_: And even if it would not cook without the aid of the non-Jew. I am astonished — behold, it is stated explicitly in the Gemara: rather, if the non-Jew had not turned it over, it would not have been cooked — why is it permitted? And Beit Yosef brought it; and so Darkei Moshe in the name of Beit Yosef: if it would not cook without stoking of a non-Jew, it is forbidden; and so it is stated explicitly in the Gemara — end of his words. And one must say that this means it would not cook properly without the aid of a non-Jew, but as maachal ben drusai it would be cooked; but in truth, in any case we establish that there are disputants whom the Rama brought below, that lighting a fire or stoking is effective; and in such a case it would certainly not be cooked if not for the act of the non-Jew. And similarly the Ran challenged those who permit that a Jew bring coals and place them in the oven to light the fire afterward. And it appears to my humble opinion that they hold that when the Gemara afterward says it is not forbidden until the beginning and end are in the hand of a non-Jew, it retracted this view; and although without a non-Jew it would not cook, nevertheless since a Jew aided at the beginning or end, it is permitted. And it appears to my humble opinion for practical law that only in a Jewish home may one rely on this leniency of "there are disputants" of the Rama below, since there is a view at the beginning of this siman in the Tur in the name of R' Avraham that in a Jewish home there is no prohibition of parched grain, although Rabbeinu Tam disagrees — nevertheless in such a case it would be permitted; but in a non-Jew's home one should not be lenient, only that the Jew should place the pot in the place fit for cooking.
turei-zahav.7#א: Except for bread. In the Ran it is written the reason that heating the oven for bread is a special labor, and Beit Yosef brings it — end of his words. It appears his explanation is that for bread one must kindle the oven and remove all the coals before baking the bread, which is not so for other dishes — one kindles the fire while the dish cooks and constantly adds; therefore a Jew's action is not so recognizable.
turei-zahav.7#ב: And there are disputants, etc. I already wrote what appears to my humble opinion on this; and likewise on what the Rama wrote here, and even stoking without intention — I wrote below that Issur ve-Heter disagrees, and Darkei Moshe wrote that the same applies to blowing on the fire with the mouth — it is effective.
turei-zahav.8#_: And she removed it, and a non-Jew came and returned it. It is not specifically that a Jew removed it, but the same law if a non-Jew removed it for some need he has in this and returned it — it is forbidden, as proven in seif 11: if it is certain that a non-Jew removed it before it reached maachal ben drusai, it is forbidden. And it appears to me that all the more so it is forbidden when a non-Jew removes it, since the non-Jew himself nullified the Jew's action and renewed everything — he uprooted the name of Israel from this labor, and this is worse than when it was uprooted automatically by a Jew. And even if you say it is worse if a Jew removed it, nevertheless it is not difficult why it did not teach a novelty here that even if a non-Jew removed it, it is forbidden — one may say it teaches that even when a Jew removes it, the prohibition is only before it reached maachal ben drusai and not afterward. And in vain did Maharach, may his memory be blessed, toil to reconcile these two seifim with each other; and what he wrote there that b'dieved it is permitted if a non-Jew removed and returned — one may not rely on this at all, for this matter was straightforward to the Rashba in the Arukh that it is forbidden; he only brought proof from the explanation of Rabbeinu Chananel that we are not concerned for this out of doubt, since it is a rabbinic matter; and so Beit Yosef wrote, and so the Tur — the implication is thus, that only in doubt they were lenient, but not when certain; and it is reasonable that whatever lost its prior action, new aspects came here, and it is actual bishul akum, and every case is equal — forbidden; and so wrote in Perishah and Levush.
turei-zahav.9#_: And there are those who permit in every case. For only for leniency do we say that as maachal ben drusai it is considered cooked so that a non-Jew will not forbid it afterward; but for stringency, no — and it still helps if a Jew finishes it afterward.
turei-zahav.11#_: And likewise every doubt, etc. He explains: that there is a doubt whether a Jew stoked the fire or not.
turei-zahav.12#א: And if a non-Jew roasted them, etc. For since they are eaten as they are when raw through salting, there is no [prohibition] of bishul akum in them; and for salting at the outset they did not decree — they only decreed on cooking by fire. And one could object: behold, even by fire there is no bishul akum here, for the Gemara says small fish do not rise on the king's table. Beit Yosef resolved that after salting they rise. Rashal resolved that they are not completely small. Maharach, may his memory be blessed, resolved that the species of those fish is always small and they are significant; but the species that grows large afterward does not rise as long as they are small.
turei-zahav.12#ב: And salted meat, etc. In the Tur he counts salted meat with small fish, and it appears he deals with where they salted greatly and it stood a long time in salt, as the Tur concludes on this until they are fit to be eaten thus without cooking.
turei-zahav.14#_: An egg, etc. The reason is that eating it is by pressing; and even those who permit in seif 12 with large fish agree here, and with bitter dates in seif 15 — for here they are not eaten except by great pressing; and so the Tur explicitly concludes "by great pressing." Darkei Moshe wrote in the name of the gloss of Alfasi, chapter of Ein Ma'amidin: those large nuts that they spice with their bitter peel and pits are forbidden because of bishul akum, for they are not eaten raw and rise on the king's table — end of his words.
turei-zahav.16#_: A non-Jew who cooked for a sick person, etc. These are the words of the Ran in the name of the Rae, whom Beit Yosef brought. And behold in Bedek HaBayit of the Rae, daf 89, he also wrote thus; and the author of Mishmeret HaBayit, who is the Rashba, wrote on this: Heaven forbid and forfend that it was not permitted even for the sick person himself except in time of need alone, namely on Shabbos; but after Shabbos it returns to its prohibition, and how much more so for a healthy person. And it is comparable to nevelah for a sick person where there is danger — it is permitted to him on Shabbos, and if he recovers it is forbidden, for every rabbinic enactment is modeled on Torah law — end of his words, and his words are correct. And there is further proof from siman 112 seif 5, that where no professional baker is available they permitted even homeowners' [bread]; and this is certainly that after he comes to a place where a professional baker is available, the bread of homeowners returns to prohibition, for it specified "where there is no professional baker," specifically; and the same applies here. And if the Beit Yosef and Rama had seen Mishmeret HaBayit, they would not have ruled for leniency like the Rae in this. And more astounding: at the end of siman 123 Beit Yosef wrote the responsum of the Ran that we do not rule like the Rae in this — and see there on the Rama's words.

siftei-kohen.1#א: ["And also rises on the king's table, etc. Since the Mechaber did not stipulate that it must be changed from its natural state by fire, it is clear that he holds that even if it was not changed, it is forbidden — and like the view of the Rambam whom he brought in Beit Yosef; and so the view of the Rav in Darkei Moshe and in Turei Chayim, general rule 71, halachah 9; and this is his view in the gloss, seif 2, that he only permitted the peas because they do not rise on the king's table, and not because they were not changed from their nature, as written in Darkei Moshe and Turei Chayim there. But in truth the essence of the Gemara appears (at the end of Avodah Zarah daf 37) like the Ran and Rashi, that it is not forbidden because of bishul akum except when changed from its nature by fire; and so in Hagahot Alfasi, chapter of Avodah Zarah; and so appears the view of the Rif, as the Ran wrote; and so appears the view of Raavan, siman 53. However, the view of other poskim appears that one should not distinguish in this:"]
siftei-kohen.1#ב: ["Rises on the king's table. Issur ve-Heter wrote: gizzards, crop, and innards — even though we said above (siman 87) their food is not human food and is not a piece worthy of honor — nevertheless they are forbidden because of bishul akum; and he brings Darkei Moshe; and he wrote further that herbs and mushrooms rise on the king's table as relish, and there is in them [the prohibition of] bishul akum; and so in Turei Chayim there at the end of halachah 15:"]
siftei-kohen.2#א: ["And so they practiced leniency with them, etc. And it is written in Turei Chayim at the beginning of general rule 35 that they practice leniency in the community of Krakow to buy whole nuts (called shtendlen nussen) that gentiles cook — end of his words; and so in the simanim of Turei Chayim, general rule 74, halachah 16, that they are permitted because they do not rise on the king's table:"]
siftei-kohen.2#ב: ["For usually they are not same-day. As below, siman 122:"]
siftei-kohen.3#א: ["Pastida. Of fish. So it is among the poskim. And Mahara of Tikotin wrote in the margin of Mordechai, chapter of Avodah Zarah: those fats of meat or of goose — usually they are already rendered, and there is no [prohibition of] bishul akum, for there is no cooking after cooking — end of his words. And if a non-Jew baked pastida with raw fat of meat, its law is like fat of fish, and it is straightforward:"]
siftei-kohen.3#ב: ["Even for one who practices leniency with bread of a non-Jew. And this is with pastida of a non-Jew; but pastida of a Jew that gentiles baked — they did not practice leniency in any place, as above in siman 112, small note 16. And the same applies: you find this law with pastida of a Jew that a non-Jew baked and made it fit with a chip, which helps for bread as above in siman 112, seif 11, and does not help for bishul akum according to the Mechaber in seif 7; but according to what the Rav wrote there, that even for cooking of a non-Jew a chip helps — you do not find this law except with pastida of a non-Jew; and so R' Peretz in Semak, siman 207:"]
siftei-kohen.4#_: With our maidservants. Those acquired by us — for the labor of a gentile's slave is a Jew's, and he is warned about it on Shabbos from the Torah, and he is not included among [gentiles] — end of his words, responsum of the Ramban whom Beit Yosef brought, and Darkei Moshe; and with those maidservants the Mechaber deals. But not with our maidservants in these lands, who are not acquired by us but only hired for a year, and we are not warned about them on Shabbos, as explained in Orach Chayim siman 344; and so the Bach. And accordingly, what the Rav wrote that b'dieved one may rely on those who permit — this does not speak of our maidservants. And one must say that he refers to the maidservants the Mechaber deals with, or that one may rely on those who permit bishul akum in a Jewish home — and this is the view of R' Avraham whom the Tur brought; and so in Darkei Moshe and Turei Chayim, general rule 71, halachah 17, in the name of Issur ve-Heter — and this is in Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, halachah 13. Or the Rav was not precise in this, for the essence of the matter relies on the reason that it is impossible that one of the household will not stoke a little. And see in Or Torah of Maharshal, siman 87, who brings the responsum of the Ramban, siman 249: some of our teachers permit with maidservants because the prohibition of bishul akum applies only to one who acts willingly, because of the decree of feasts; but these maidservants and slaves of ours act under compulsion, whether they wish or not — there is no closeness of mind; nevertheless their words are not clear and we do not rely on this, and we practice prohibition even b'dieved — end of his words; and so in the responsum of the Rashba, siman 68. And accordingly one may say that the reasoning of the one who permits whom the Mechaber wrote is for this reason, and therefore the Rav wrote that one may rely on them b'dieved; except that in Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe this reason is not mentioned.
siftei-kohen.6#_: And even if it would not, etc. It appears difficult, for it is against the Gemara in Avodah Zarah (daf 38 side 1), and Beit Yosef brings that we say: if the non-Jew did not turn it over in it, it would not be cooked — it is bishul akum and forbidden; and so among the poskim and Beit Yosef; and also in Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, halachah 9: if a Jew placed meat on coals where it was not fit to cook and roast, and a non-Jew came and turned it over and it cooked — permitted — end of his words; requires study. And it appears that Issur ve-Heter and the Rav hold that although by Gemara law it is forbidden in such a case, nevertheless also stoking and a chip are forbidden by Gemara law, for it would not cook without the aid of the non-Jew, and nevertheless we permit — only because we establish that just as a chip helps above in siman 112, seif 10, so too for bishul akum, as the Rif wrote in Semak and Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43. And if so, just as a chip for bread is not permitted by Gemara law, as the poskim wrote in siman 112, but we rely on what is written in Hilchot Minhagim between the people of Eretz Yisrael and Babylonia that it helps, and "leave Israel to be unwitting," etc., as the Rosh and Tur wrote in siman 112 — so too for bishul akum; and so the Ramban whom the Ran brought, chapter of Avodah Zarah — see there. And accordingly, that which the Rav did not emend anything in seif 10 against the Mechaber's words is because he relied on what he wrote before; and it is possible to say that here we deal where the Jew placed the coals, therefore even though it would not cook without the aid of the non-Jew it is permitted, for it is like lighting the fire in the gloss of seif 7 that is permitted — the reason being since the Jew made the flame. And below seif 10 deals where the non-Jew placed the coals, and therefore even though the Jew placed the meat on the coals, since it would not cook without the aid of the non-Jew, it is forbidden; but in Issur ve-Heter and Turei Chayim there it appears permitted in every case — see there; and also here it appears it is only permitted because the Jew placed the meat on the coals — investigate. And nevertheless for practical law requires study, since the Gemara states explicitly that where a Jew placed meat on coals and a non-Jew came and turned it over, it is forbidden if it would not cook without the aid of the non-Jew, and so the poskim — except that Issur ve-Heter and the Rav are lenient in this, and because they compare them to a chip and stoking; and one may say there is a dispute regarding a chip and stoking, as the Ran explicitly distinguishes there, chapter of Avodah Zarah — see there.
siftei-kohen.7#א: ["Or stoking, etc. And Issur ve-Heter wrote there: but one should be careful when stoking coals that this stoking should help repair the fire and help hasten its cooking by a Jew — end of his words; and so it appears in the Gemara and poskim that we require the Jew to do an approximation of cooking:"]
siftei-kohen.7#ב: ["And even stoking without intention, etc. And in the gloss at the end of Sefer Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, he ruled that one must intend to aid in repairing the fire to make it fit:"]
siftei-kohen.7#ג: ["And he did not throw a chip there, etc. It implies; but if he threw a chip, it helps also for bishul akum; and so it is in Semak and Issur ve-Heter explicitly:"]
siftei-kohen.8#א: ["And she removed it. It is not specifically that a Jew removed it, but the same if a non-Jew removed it and returned it — forbidden, as the Rashba and Taz wrote in seif 10; and some say; and in the Bach he lengthy refuted and built and distinguished on this, and his view is that when a non-Jew removed and returned it, it is permitted; and I have [grounds] to answer his words, and here is not the place to lengthen; for according to what we establish, that even if a Jew lit the fire or threw a chip it is permitted, it makes no difference in this, for it is obvious that it is permitted; and although I wrote in small note 8 in the name of the Ran that there is room to distinguish, nevertheless here, since only the non-Jew removed and not the Jew, it appears it is nevertheless comparable to a chip, and such is the case:"]
siftei-kohen.8#ב: ["Forbidden. Since it was cooked by a non-Jew without an approximation of cooking by a Jew — so we say in the Gemara and poskim:"]
siftei-kohen.9#_: And there are those who permit. And so agreed most poskim, and not like Maharshal in his Or Torah.
siftei-kohen.11#_: And he left a non-Jew to guard it. And this is in a matter where there is no concern that the non-Jew switched them — so among the poskim, and it is straightforward; and see above siman 118, seif 10.
siftei-kohen.12#א: ["Small fish, etc. Tosafot and other poskim wrote that this means even somewhat large; for if completely small — behold, we say in the Gemara that even if small fish were cooked, there is no [prohibition of] bishul akum in them, for they do not rise on the king's table. The Bach wrote that when small fish do not rise on the king's table, that is with small fish whose growth is large, and those fish in their small state are not significant and do not rise on the king's table; but small fish whose growth is always small are significant and rise on the king's table; and he brought proofs — see there:"]
siftei-kohen.12#ב: ["And likewise anything, etc. And Issur ve-Heter wrote that beets and chestnuts (called in foreign tongue castan) are not eaten raw except by pressing, and there is in them [the prohibition of] bishul akum; and in Turei Chayim, general rule 71, at the end of halachah 15, he wrote on this that it does not appear [so] with chestnuts, for in all these lands most of their eating is raw — end of his words; and see in the glosses at the end of Sefer Issur ve-Heter what he wrote to distinguish regarding chestnuts:"]
siftei-kohen.13#_: And smoked is not like cooked. Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe wrote; but it appears that even though a Jew made them, if a non-Jew cooked them it is forbidden, similar to large fish below — end of his words. And it appears it appears to refer also to small fish; but in Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, halachah 16, he wrote that small fish — even if a non-Jew smoked them and afterward cooked them — are permitted, for smoking is equivalent in all its kinds to salting — see there. And accordingly, for those who permit in seif 12 large salted fish that a non-Jew cooked, the same applies to large smoked fish that a non-Jew cooked — they are permitted; and so the Bach in a later pamphlet.
siftei-kohen.15#_: Dates, etc. Issur ve-Heter wrote, general rule 43, halachah 3: however, these pears and apples — even though most of their eating is by roasting and cooking, if a non-Jew roasted and cooked them they are permitted, for they are nevertheless also eaten raw, and moreover most of the essence of their eating is raw — until here.
siftei-kohen.16#א: ["Vessels in which cooked, etc. And it is written in Turei Chayim, general rule 71, halachah 14, as follows: and vessels in which gentiles cooked are forbidden; therefore one must be careful with gentile maidservants who cook for themselves in the rabbi's house that they not place [food] on the fire; and if they preceded and placed it, etc., hagalah is required — end of his words. And one cannot challenge: behold, he wrote there halachah 17 that b'dieved they practice to permit even a dish cooked in a Jewish home — one may say as written in the gloss at the end of Sefer Issur ve-Heter: even though she cooked in a Jewish home, if she cooks for herself it is worse; and although inside Turei Chayim he permits in a Jewish home because it is impossible that one of the household will stoke — one may say that if she cooks for herself there is no custom at all that one of the household will stoke:"]
siftei-kohen.16#ב: ["Require kashering, etc. And if it was cooked in them b'dieved and there is a majority in the dish, it is permitted, for bishul akum [prohibitions] are nullified in the majority, as above in siman 112, small note 23, and above in siman 115, small note 17:"]

kaf-hachayim.1#_: 1) [Seif 1] A food that is not eaten as it is when raw, etc. — and the reason is that the essence of the decree is because of [intermarriage] feasts, and a thing that is not so important — a person does not invite his friend for it. Taz, small note 1. Lechem HaPanim, note 1; Binyamin Zeev, note 1. And according to this reason, the cooking of an apostate is permitted, for there is no [concern of] feasts; except that there is another reason explained in Beit Yosef, lest he feed him forbidden things; and accordingly, the cooking of an apostate is also forbidden, for he is like a denier of the entire Torah, and lest he feed him forbidden things — Sefer Tiferet Moshe. And accordingly, the same applies to an apostate who desecrates Shabbos in public, or [denies] the entire Torah except for two [commandments], whose law is like a non-Jew, as above siman 2 seif 5, and below siman 119 — his cooking is likewise forbidden. Pit'hei Teshuvah, note 1. And it is found that this matter is disputed according to the reasons; and if so, since it is a rabbinic matter, it appears that b'dieved one should not forbid. And see above siman 112, note 11.
kaf-hachayim.2#_: 2) There. And also rises on the king's table, etc. — it is not specifically kings, but even if it rises on the table of ministers in that land, it is forbidden. Rabbeinu HaAri, z"l, in Sefer Ta'amei HaMitzvot, parashat Ekev, and in Sha'ar HaMitzvot, parashat Vayelech. Birkei Yosef in Shivhei Yosef, note 2 — and he means important people to whom this food is fit to be given.
kaf-hachayim.3#_: 3) There. And also rises on the king's table, etc. — and one should not distinguish between a thing changed from its nature or not; and so Issur ve-Heter (general rule 43, halachah 1); and so agreed other poskim, and not like the Ran. Torat Chatat, general rule 71, halachah 16. Shach, small note 1. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef, note 18. Peri Chadash, note 1. Peri Toar, note 1. Minchat Yitzchak on Torat Chatat there, note 32. Erech HaShulchan, notes 2 and 4. She'erit Yosef, note 1. Arukh HaShulchan, note 9.
kaf-hachayim.4#_: 4) Gizzards, crop, and innards — even though we say (Nedarim 54 side 2) their food is not human food and is not a piece worthy of honor — nevertheless they are forbidden because of bishul akum. Issur ve-Heter, general rule 43, halachah 2. Darkei Moshe, note 2. Shach, small note 2. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef, note 16. Peri Chadash, note 2. Lechem HaPanim, note 1. Binyamin Zeev, note 1. Arukh HaShulchan, note 10. Zivchei Tzedek, note 3.
kaf-hachayim.5#_: 5) And even herbs and mushrooms have [the prohibition of] bishul akum, for they rise as relish. Issur ve-Heter there. Torat Chatat there. Darkei Moshe there. Shach there. Knesset HaGedolah there. Chochmat Adam, klal 66, note 4. However, Peri Chadash at the end of note 3 disagrees and wrote that herbs and mushrooms do not rise on the king's table and there is no [prohibition of] bishul akum; and so agreed Arukh HaShulchan, note 10. And Peri Toar, note 7, wrote that in our places herbs and mushrooms rise on the king's table and are for improvement, as Issur ve-Heter's view; and what Peri Chadash rejected from the Gemara is no proof, for nowadays they do rise — and everything is according to the place. And so Minchat Yitzchak in Sulam at the end of Torat Chatat, general rule 71, halachah 16. And so Birkei Yosef in Shivhei Yosef, note 9, in the name of Radak, that everything is according to place and time. And so Chochmat Adam there. And see below, note 10 and note 11.
kaf-hachayim.6#_: 6) Chestnuts (called in Arabic kastana) that a gentile picked are permitted, for they are eaten as they are when raw, even though most of their eating is by roasting and cooking. Birkei Yosef there, note 8, in the name of Radak. However, Peri Chadash, note 22, brought a dispute whether they are eaten raw; and therefore we follow this according to place and time, as written in the previous note: if most of that place eat them raw, there is no [prohibition of] bishul akum; if not, there is bishul akum.
kaf-hachayim.7#_: 7) There. Or as relish, etc. — so the Tur; and it appears he means that even though kings do not dip bread in it, since it rises on their table as relish — that is, to conclude a meal — it is forbidden because of bishul akum. Peri Chadash, note 3. However, he disagrees on this and holds that things that come to conclude a meal that are not made to dip bread in them have no [prohibition of] bishul akum — see there. But Chochmat Adam, klal 66, note 1, wrote that a thing that comes to conclude a meal has [the prohibition of] bishul akum. And so Arukh HaShulchan, note 7: the view of the Tur and Shulchan Aruch is that when the Sages said "to dip bread in it," it is not specifically so, and it is the way of the matter — they said that an unimportant thing does not rise on the king's table to dip bread in it; but the essence depends on a thing of importance that rises on the king's table even if eaten by itself and not with bread; and he concluded that for practical law, since the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled to forbid, so we conclude.
kaf-hachayim.8#_: 8) A rice dish has [the prohibition of] bishul akum. Peri Chadash there, and note 5. Lechem HaPanim, note 5. Binyamin Zeev, at the end of note 5. Chochmat Adam there, note 2. Zivchei Tzedek, note 5.
kaf-hachayim.9#_: 9) Porridge (wheat or barley groats) has no [prohibition of] bishul akum. Peri Chadash, note 5. Lechem HaPanim there. Kehillat Yehudah, seif 1. Erech HaShulchan, note 3. Chochmat Adam there. Zivchei Tzedek, note 6. And see below, note 63 and note 64. And it appears that rice called hirz is also not served on the king's table. Chochmat Adam there. [And see above, note 8.]
kaf-hachayim.10#_: 10) A food eaten as it is when raw, and one person cannot eat it except roasted or cooked — his view is nullified before all people, since most of the world eat it as it is when raw, and it is permitted for him too; and likewise the reverse: if the majority do not eat it as it is when raw, even though this person eats it as it is when raw, there is [the prohibition of] bishul akum, and for him too it is forbidden. Responsa of the Rikash called Ohalei Yaakov, siman 58. Peri Chadash, note 3. Minchat Yitzchak in Sulam at the end of Torat Chatat, general rule 71, halachah 16. Lechem HaPanim, note 2. Binyamin Zeev, note 2. Birkei Yosef in Shivhei Yosef, note 1. Chochmat Adam there, note 4. Arukh HaShulchan, note 12. Zivchei Tzedek, note 8.
kaf-hachayim.11#_: 11) And if there are places that eat them raw and places that do not eat them raw — each follows his place. Peri Chadash there. Sulam there. Lechem HaPanim there. Binyamin Zeev there. Birkei Yosef there. Chochmat Adam there. Arukh HaShulchan there. Zivchei Tzedek, note 9.
kaf-hachayim.12#_: 12) And an important person must be stringent with bishul akum even with a thing eaten as it is when raw, as we say in Shabbos daf 51 side 1. Maharikash in glosses on the Shulchan Aruch; and so Shach below, siman 152, small note 2. However, Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef in this siman, note 14, lengthy on this and wrote that even an important person need not be stringent in this. And so Peri Chadash at the end of note 3. Lechem HaPanim, note 2. Peri Toar below, siman 114, note 70. Erech HaShulchan, note 3. Derech Emunah. Arukh HaShulchan, note 11. However, Rav Mazmor le-David in this siman wrote that for practical law an important person should be stringent, since the Rif and Rosh copied there that statement of R' Ami as well — end of his words. And so from the words of the Ari, z"l, written in the note afterward that one should be stringent. And so the view of Birkei Yosef in Shivhei Yosef, note 4. And see further in our words in Orach Chayim, siman 257, note 34.
kaf-hachayim.13#_: 13) Lupines have no [prohibition of] bishul akum. Rambam, chapter 17 of Hilchot Maachalot Assurot, halachah 15. Peri Chadash, note 2. And because of gentile vessels (meaning: that it was cooked in their intestines) it is a dispute, and one should be stringent. Maharal, siman 138. Maharikash in glosses on the Shulchan Aruch. However, what he wrote "and because of gentile vessels," etc. — see below siman 122, seif 6, and in the gloss that wrote that if he cooked for him, it is permitted to buy from him l'chatchila — see there. However, Rabbeinu HaAri, z"l, in Sha'ar HaMitzvot, parashat Vayelech, wrote that one must be careful not to eat lupines boiled by gentiles for seasoning; and although by law they are permitted because they do not rise on the king's table, nevertheless he is not inferior to that man (see Moed Katan daf 12 side 2) to whom Eliyahu, z"l, did not appear because he drank water that his Aramean brother gave him — end of his words. However, what he wrote "by law they are permitted," etc. — this is if he cooked in a Jewish vessel or in his vessel to sell to a non-Jew; but if he cooked in his vessel to sell to a Jew, by law it is forbidden because of gentile vessels, as will be explained in our words there — see there.
kaf-hachayim.14#_: 14) Milk that a gentile cooked and made into cheese has no [concern of] bishul akum. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef, note 26. Binyamin Zeev, note 5.
kaf-hachayim.15#_: 15) Cheese has no [prohibition of] bishul akum, since it is eaten as it is when raw; and even a person who does not eat cheese raw — if it was cooked by a non-Jew, it is permitted for him, for his view is nullified before all people. Maharikash in the responsa called Ohalei Yaakov, siman 58. Birkei Yosef, note 1; and so above, note 10, in the name of several poskim — see there.
kaf-hachayim.16#_: 16) There. That a non-Jew cooked it, etc. — whether cooking of a pot or cooking of roasting; for roasting too is called cooking, as stated in Divrei HaYamim: "and they cooked the Pesach"; and so it is proven in the Gemara from the case of a gentile who singed the head of his ship, and from the case of a Jew who placed meat on coals. And so the Rashba in Torat HaBayit. Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Tur, note 1. Peri Chadash, note 1. And so it is proven below, seif 12.

beur-hagra.1#א: A thing, etc., and also, etc. As Tosafot wrote there: the latter version adds to the former version, since it says there is between them, etc., and it did not enumerate how many things rise on the table of kings and are eaten raw; and so holds the Ran in the fourth chapter of Shabbos; and R' Yosef there, etc.; and so in chapter 2 of Rambam on R' Yehudah HaNasi: if because he drank, etc.; and so the plain Gemara in Avodah Zarah 38 side 2 and 39 side 2: if because of bishul akum, etc.; and the halachah follows the latter version of Rabbi Yochanan — he holds like him, as written, Niddah 49a and Yevamos 46a; and see Tosafot there and there.
beur-hagra.1#ג: Or, etc. Tur; and as written there: a non-Jew who kindled, etc. — only because of bishul akum; and Rambam explained that they come as relish.
beur-hagra.1#ד: Even, etc. Rashi 35 side 2, s.v. vehashlakot.
beur-hagra.1#ה: And in a house. Tosafot 38a, s.v. ella, etc.
beur-hagra.2#א: And permitted, etc. As written 37b: wheat that one made into parched grain is permitted, and the same applies to these; and as Rambam wrote that a person does not invite his friend for parched grain — and therefore it is not, etc. (Collection) And permitted, etc., and likewise, etc. Gemara 37b, 38b: the baraita, etc., and parched grain; and likewise of legumes, as written, the latter, etc., in Talfachi, etc. (until here). (Collection) And permitted, etc., that they are not, etc. Rambam; and in the Gemara (37b) they said because they were not changed, etc.; and Rambam holds that for the conclusion that it is not derived from a verse, therefore one must say because of this reason; but the Ran wrote that the above reason that it was not changed remains, since they relied on a verse — we require a similarity to the verse (and in the end of chapter 4 of Shabbos and chapter 2 of Moed Katan — requires study); and so Rashi 35b, s.v. vehachamin, etc., and s.v. vekalyot, etc.; and the Ran wrote: except that I have not seen among the early authorities who explained that everything that was not changed by fire is permitted (until here).
beur-hagra.2#ב: And all fruits, etc. As written there 38b in oil, even though they were at first olives. Darkei Moshe.
beur-hagra.3#_: And likewise vegetables, etc. Meaning: even though the fat is not visible and the first taste of Tosafot — which applies when visible — does not apply; and therefore "and it is absorbed," etc.
beur-hagra.4#א: There are those, etc. Since they are acquired to a Jew for practical labor of his hands, and he is warned about them on Shabbos from the Torah — they are not included among them; and the decree of feasts applies only to one who acts willingly, for it is closeness of mind; and he transgressed Shabbos, siman 68.
beur-hagra.4#ב: And there are, etc. This is the Rashba; and proof from what they challenge Nazir 57a according to Rav: from minor slaves; and if it were so, since they do not know the nature of idolatry, it is forbidden only because of feasts — therefore it is forbidden only in their drinking according to Rav, and not with maidservants and slaves — it does not apply.
beur-hagra.4#ג: And b'dieved, etc. Combined with the view of the Raavad in Tosafot 38a, s.v. ella. Darkei Moshe in the name of Issur ve-Heter.
beur-hagra.4#ד: And even, etc., because, etc. And as written in chapter 7 in the gloss: and there are disputants, etc., and even, etc.
beur-hagra.5#ב: But, etc. There, from what he wrote: for bishul akum.
beur-hagra.6#א: Every, etc. There side 2: whether he placed, etc., and it is not, etc.
beur-hagra.6#ב: And even, etc. In the Gemara the opposite is explained — except that if he did not turn over, etc.; and so in chapter 10 and Asheri and Peri Chadash.
beur-hagra.7#א: There is no, etc. As written: except that if he did not, etc.; and the same here; and therefore there: a Jew places, etc. — specifically placing.
beur-hagra.7#ב: And there are disputants, etc. According to the Tur's explanation of what is written there: a Jew stoked coals, and even if it would cook without a Jew's stoking; and as written there: if a non-Jew finished it is permitted; if he finished, etc.; and it appears similar to if a non-Jew finished it is permitted; and the reason as the Ran wrote: approximations of cooking are a matter; as written in chapter 2 of Shevuos that approximations of labor are labor in such a case — see there 17b — except that for leniency they said here it is not a [significant] matter, and we learn that lighting the fire also helps; and it is not so that only if a Jew finishes in such a case it helps but not at the beginning, as written: except that if he did not turn over, etc.; and see Ran.
beur-hagra.7#ג: And some say, etc. See above that even lighting does not help.
beur-hagra.7#ד: And he did not throw, etc. This helps, as the Ran wrote: since an approximation of cooking helps like finishing.
beur-hagra.8#_: That it is, etc. Rashi, first chapter of Shabbos.
beur-hagra.9#א: If they cooked it, etc. As written: everything that was cooked as maachal ben drusai, etc., even though he placed it on a tile; and the same applies to the reverse.
beur-hagra.9#ב: And there are those who permit, etc. As written there: until the beginning and end are, etc.; and only for leniency they said "everything," etc., like approximations of cooking as above; and the first version holds this is called "finishing"; and nevertheless he relied on this view in the Shulchan Aruch on erev [Shabbos], etc. (Collection) And there are those who permit, etc.: according to the first view as written, and a Jew turned it over — it should have said until it did not reach maachal ben drusai; but in Terumat HaDeshen 90b he decided it is forbidden from what is written: this non-Jew singed, etc. — it appears that if he intended for cooking it is forbidden, even though it is impossible that by singeing it becomes fully roasted (until here).
beur-hagra.10#א: He placed, etc. Gemara there: except that if, etc.
beur-hagra.10#ב: As maachal ben drusai. As above, that after maachal ben drusai, even if he placed it on a tile, as written there.
beur-hagra.11#_: He placed, etc., and there is no, etc. From what we say: he places, etc., and one is not concerned — thus we are not concerned for this.
beur-hagra.12#א: Fish, etc. Wording of the Rambam until "permitted."
beur-hagra.12#ב: Or a non-Jew. And so the Rosh in chapter 2 of Yoreh De'ah; and as written in seif 13 regarding salting, etc.
beur-hagra.12#ג: And if, etc. Like our text; and so the text of the Rif and Rosh: gentiles roasted them, etc.
beur-hagra.12#ד: But, etc. There side 2: a salted fish, etc.; and according to the Raavad and Ramban: with salting by a non-Jew — some say permitted only if gentiles roasted them, and he explains like Rabbi Yochanan; and as Abaye said there. (Collection) But salted fish, etc.: like Rabbi Yochanan, whom Rav holds like, who said salted small fish are not, etc. — but large ones are forbidden. Ran in the name of Rabbeinu Yonah (until here).
beur-hagra.12#ה: And there are those who permit. As the Rif and Rosh wrote in the name of a Gaon: Abaye refers only to an egg; but for fish we return to the general rule, and his words are not, etc.; and moreover his teachers were not like Rabbeinu Yonah; and so he wondered in Terumat HaDeshen.
beur-hagra.12#ו: And so he ruled, etc. As written in the Shulchan Aruch: but, etc., they are not, etc. — and this is from Terumat HaDeshen, who distinguished between them and small fish; and as written in the Gemara in small fried fish; and as written in Semak.
beur-hagra.12#ז: And meat, etc. Even though they are permitted to be moved, as written in chapter 18 of Shabbos (128a) — likewise they permit there bland meat; and nevertheless we say here: a Jew placed, etc.; and likewise an egg that is fit to be swallowed; and as written in seif 14.
beur-hagra.13#א: A fish, etc. All this is the wording of the Rambam; and according to Rashi: with salting by a non-Jew they dispute, and he explains like Chizkiyah and bar Kafra, as above.
beur-hagra.13#ב: And fruits, etc. Yerushalmi, chapter 6 of Nedarim.
beur-hagra.13#ג: That salted, etc., also, etc. There 40b: the baraita: locusts, etc. — even though if gentiles roasted them it is forbidden, as written 38a; and the same for salting; and even the Raavad and Ramban rule thus — except they hold there is a dispute in this, as above. (Collection) A fish, etc., that salted, etc.: as written in the Mishnah 39b: and pickling that is not their way, etc.; and there 37b: rather like water, etc., by fire; and even though this answer does not stand, nevertheless there is a dispute on it for practical law, and not like Rashi 38b, s.v. dag, etc.; and even according to Rashi we establish like those who permit, as written in seif 12. Terumat HaDeshen (until here).
beur-hagra.14#_: Even though fit, etc. As written in the first chapter of Yoreh De'ah (4 side 2).
beur-hagra.15#_: That they are not, etc. See Rashi there.
beur-hagra.16#א: Vessels, etc. As with all prohibitions of their [rabbinic] decrees that forbid their mixture — such as the oil of the gid, as written above siman 65 seif 9, and in siman 100 seif 2, and udder in siman 90, and broth of non-kosher fish in siman 83; and we say in Chullin (99b) that according to R' Yochanan it forbids nearly two hundred, and according to the Tanna Kamma until 495, as written in chapter 10 of Terumot; and we say in Chullin (98a): do not treat lightly, etc.; and likewise terumah of chutz la'aretz — according to Tosafot it forbids up to 101; and other prohibitions.
beur-hagra.16#ב: And some say it is not needed. For the decree of feasts does not apply in such a case; and it appears there is proof for his words from siman 112 seif 14; but it is not so, for regarding ipinadeh he forbids there seif 6, and here seif 16; and so the Rashba brought proof from ipinadeh that he forbids because of feasts. (Collection) And some say it is not needed: and so Nekudot HaKesef, end of chapter 8 of Yevamos — see there (until here).
beur-hagra.16#ג: And even, etc., if it is, etc. As written in Yerushalmi, first chapter of Terumot: it teaches, R' Chalifta ben Shaul: a pot in which terumah was cooked — one purges it in boiling water three times and that suffices. R' Ba said: and one does not learn from it regarding nevelah. R' Yosi challenged before R' Ba: terumah [entails] death penalty and nevelah [entails] lashes — and you say thus? He said to him: as those who say they accepted the tithes upon themselves of their own accord. Meaning: since it is rabbinic, they were lenient even though the Torah testified about the twenty-four [priestly gifts], etc. R' Yusti ben Shunam asked before R' Mana: we learned: if one pressed and squeezed it, behold it is terumah — and you say thus? Meaning: thus it is clear they were not lenient in it even in a slight matter. He said to him: here it is purged by fire and departs. Meaning: this is not so much of a leniency. And the Rashba wrote: and the same applies to all prohibitions of their decrees; but in prohibitions of their decrees that have no Torah root, like terumah nowadays, [one may be lenient]; but in prohibitions that have a Torah root, no — for blood that was salted is forbidden only rabbinically, as written in chapter 23 of Menachot (21b), and nevertheless R' Ami broke that bowl in Pesachim (111b); and therefore "because," etc.; and see Nekudot HaKesef in Bava Batra, chapter 8a.
beur-hagra.16#ד: A non-Jew, etc. So the Rae; and according to his view that whatever the decree of feasts does not apply to is permitted; but the Rashba disagreed with him, and the Taz and Peri Chadash.
